title: Normal forms: 1NF, 2NF and 3NF on one messy table

authoring.author: Parikshaa content team
authoring.originality: Written for Parikshaa: our own canteen example of normalisation, examples, code, quiz and explanations; no text from any site, book or course.

outcomes: can spot update, insert and delete anomalies in a table
can write the functional dependencies of a small table and find its key
can take a table to 3NF and explain what each step removed

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.body: A badly shaped table works fine on day one and quietly corrupts itself by month three: a price changed in one row but not another, a warden's name spelt two ways. Normalisation is the discipline that prevents this. Placement tests ask "which normal form is this table in?", and system design interviews ask you to sketch tables; both need the same skill: **seeing which facts depend on which**.

sections.heading: The messy table
sections.body:
Our canteen started with one spreadsheet-style table, `canteen_orders`:

| order_id | roll | name | hostel | warden | items | prices |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 21CS04 | Aditi | Kaveri | Mrs Iyer | Poha, Chai×2 | 30, 10 |
| 2 | 21ME11 | Bilal | Tapti | Mr Bhosle | Samosa×3 | 15 |
| 3 | 21CS04 | Aditi | Kaveri | Mrs Iyer | Chai | 10 |

It has three kinds of trouble, called **anomalies**:

- **Update anomaly:** Kaveri gets a new warden. We must change every row of every Kaveri student; miss one and the data disagrees with itself.
- **Insert anomaly:** a new item, Upma at ₹25, cannot be recorded until somebody orders it, because there is no row to put it in.
- **Delete anomaly:** if Bilal's only order is deleted, we also lose the fact that Tapti's warden is Mr Bhosle.

All three come from one cause: **one table is storing several different facts**, so each fact is repeated or tied to unrelated data.

sections.heading: Functional dependencies: the tool
sections.body:
A **functional dependency** `X → Y` means: if two rows agree on `X`, they must agree on `Y`. Written for our canteen:

- `roll → name, hostel` (a roll number fixes the student)
- `hostel → warden`
- `item → price`
- `order_id → roll` (an order belongs to one student)
- `(order_id, item) → qty`

A **key** is a smallest set of columns that determines every other column. Once each line of an order is its own row, the key of the big table is `(order_id, item)`.

**Normal forms are rules about which dependencies may live in one table.** Each step below moves a dependency that breaks the rule into a table of its own.

sections.heading: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF
sections.body:
**1NF: one value per cell.** `items` holds a list ("Poha, Chai×2"). We split it so each row is one item of one order, with a `qty` column. Now `(order_id, item)` is the key.

**2NF: no partial dependency.** In 2NF, no non-key column may depend on **only part** of a composite key. But `price` depends on `item` alone, and `roll`, `name`, `hostel`, `warden` depend on `order_id` alone. Each part goes to its own table: `items(item, price)`, `orders(order_id, roll, ...)`, and `order_lines(order_id, item, qty)` keeps only what needs the whole key.

**3NF: no transitive dependency.** In 3NF, a non-key column may not depend on **another non-key column**. In `orders(order_id, roll, name, hostel, warden)`, `warden` depends on `hostel`, which depends on `roll`, which depends on `order_id`. We split again: `students(roll, name, hostel)` and `hostels(hostel, warden)`, leaving `orders(order_id, roll)`.

A one-line memory aid: every non-key column depends on **the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key**.

> **Note:** A table whose key is a single column is automatically in 2NF once it is in 1NF: there is no "part" of the key to depend on. Partial dependencies only appear with composite keys.

visual.alt: The steps: 1NF splits the item list into rows; 2NF moves price to items and student columns to orders; 3NF moves name and hostel to students and warden to hostels.

rows: list of items in one cell

sections.heading: The same data, rebuilt with joins
sections.body: Normalising must not lose information: joining the small tables must give back exactly what the big table said. Here are the five 3NF tables with our three orders; the query rebuilds each order's student, warden and bill.

code.src:
SELECT o.order_id, s.name, h.warden, SUM(l.qty * i.price) AS bill
FROM orders AS o
JOIN students AS s ON s.roll = o.roll
JOIN hostels AS h ON h.hostel = s.hostel
JOIN order_lines AS l ON l.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN items AS i ON i.item = l.item
GROUP BY o.order_id, s.name, h.warden
ORDER BY o.order_id;
code.expected_output:
1	Aditi	Mrs Iyer	50
2	Bilal	Mr Bhosle	45
3	Aditi	Mrs Iyer	10
code.caption: Five 3NF tables joined back into one bill per order

sections.heading: What the split bought us
sections.body:
Order 1 is Poha (₹30) plus two Chai (₹10 each), a bill of ₹50; order 2 is three Samosa, ₹45; order 3 is one Chai, ₹10. The joins give back everything the messy table had.

Now replay the anomalies:

- Kaveri's new warden: **one** row in `hostels` changes. Every bill shows it at once.
- Upma at ₹25: one insert into `items`, no order needed.
- Deleting Bilal's order: `hostels` still says Tapti's warden is Mr Bhosle.

Each fact now lives in exactly **one** place. That is the real goal; the normal forms are just a checklist for getting there.

There is a small price: the bill now needs four joins instead of one table scan. With indexes on the key columns these joins are cheap for a canteen, and a wrong bill costs far more than a few microseconds.

sections.heading: A method for exam questions
sections.body:
Placement tests often give a relation and a list of dependencies and ask for its highest normal form. A steady method beats guessing:

1. **Find the key.** Start from the columns that never appear on the right of any dependency; they must be in every key. Add columns until their closure (everything they determine, following the arrows) covers the whole table.
2. **Check 1NF.** Any lists, repeating groups or multi-part cells? If yes, stop: not even 1NF.
3. **Check 2NF** only if the key has several columns. For each dependency, is the left side a *proper part* of the key and the right side a non-key column? If so, 2NF is broken.
4. **Check 3NF.** For each dependency, is the left side something other than a key, with a non-key column on the right? If so, 3NF is broken.

Work the steps in order and write one line of reason for each. In our canteen, step 3 catches `item → price` and step 4 catches `hostel → warden`, exactly the two splits we made. The same four steps also tell you *what* to split: each broken dependency becomes a table whose key is its left side.

sections.heading: Common mix-ups
sections.body:
**Many students think more normalised is always better.** Actually each split adds a join. Read-heavy reports sometimes **denormalise** on purpose (keep the bill total in `orders`) and accept the cost of keeping copies in sync. Normalise first, then denormalise deliberately where measurements show it pays.

**Many students think 2NF is about a single-column key.** It is the opposite: 2NF only has work to do when the key has **several** columns.

**Many students think a dependency is a fact about today's rows.** It is a rule about all possible rows. That every current student in Kaveri is named Aditi does not mean `hostel → name`; ask whether the real world forces it.

sections.heading: Interview questions
sections.body: Answers as a strong candidate would say them.

qa.q: What is the difference between 2NF and 3NF?
qa.a: 2NF forbids a non-key column depending on part of a composite key. 3NF additionally forbids a non-key column depending on another non-key column, a transitive dependency. In our canteen, price depending on item alone broke 2NF, and warden depending on hostel broke 3NF.
So each fact is stored once. That removes update, insert and delete anomalies: a change is made in one place, new facts can be recorded on their own, and deleting one fact does not erase another.

When reads vastly outnumber writes and a join is a measured bottleneck, for example a dashboard total. I would keep the normalised tables as the source of truth and update the copy in the same transaction or with a trigger, so it cannot drift silently.

Boyce-Codd normal form requires that for every non-trivial dependency X → Y, X is a superkey. It is a little stricter than 3NF, which allows Y to be part of a key; most practical designs that reach 3NF are already in BCNF.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
- Anomalies (update, insert, delete) come from one table holding several facts.
- Write the functional dependencies first; they decide the split.
- 1NF: one value per cell. 2NF: no partial dependency on a composite key. 3NF: no non-key → non-key dependency.
- "The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key."
- Joins must rebuild the original data; denormalise later, on purpose.

quiz.stem: Table `marks(roll, subject, marks, subject_teacher)`, key `(roll, subject)`. `subject → subject_teacher`. Which normal form does it break?
quiz.explanation: subject_teacher depends on subject, only part of the composite key: a partial dependency, so 2NF is broken.

quiz.stem: Table `students(roll, hostel, warden)`, key `roll`, with `hostel → warden`. What is the problem?
quiz.explanation: warden depends on hostel, a non-key column: roll → hostel → warden is transitive.

quiz.stem: Deleting a student's only order also deletes the only record of her hostel's warden. Which anomaly is this?
quiz.explanation: Losing an unrelated fact when a row is deleted is a delete anomaly.

quiz.stem: A table's key is a single column and every cell holds one value. Which is certainly true?
quiz.explanation: With a single-column key there is no partial dependency, so 1NF implies 2NF; it may still break 3NF.

revision_card.front: 1NF, 2NF and 3NF in one line each, and the memory aid?
revision_card.back: 1NF: atomic cells. 2NF: no non-key column depends on part of a composite key. 3NF: no non-key column depends on another non-key column. "The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key."
